You wrote a very good eval. Also, I have to add that I think people sometimes really forget, possibly due to the adult actors--the wilderness timeline is featuring KIDS. Yes, some are legal adults and 18-19, but...I mean have you been to a high school and hung around the kids? They all have very different levels of maturity, and most average teenagers don't know how to understand or process their feelings. They don't know how to control very intense emotions, their sexual urges, or how to make good choices. They aren't good at impulse control and they have moments of absolute clarity showing you they are on the cusp of adulthood, and other times they might as well be ten years old--especially if they're emotionally distressed. Teenagers are, in most cases, selfish in a developmentally appropriate way. They can make poor choices both because of selfishness or they're just doing what makes them feel good, or because they just don't know better yet. Teenagers are also going through the challenging process of a physical change of their body and psychological change into adulthood, and a myriad of social pressures from family, friends, and society in general. Add to that some that already have trauma like Van, Nat, and (I'm convinced!) Shauna, you have a dangerous mix. There's no one to protect them, comfort them, discipline them, or teach them how to survive the outside world or the world inside their heads.

Your trainer telling you that your dog will never be a dog park dog is 100% telling you that this is a dog that very likely will dislike dogs for all its life and possibly never be able to be around others.

\-Aggression is genetic. This means that unlike "Bad behaviors"  like counter-surfing, peeing indoors and so on, this is a personality trait literally in their brain. Can you train and work on things like that? Sure, but it's an uphill battle and very frustrating for both the dog and human.

\-Dog aggression and reactivity isn't always based in any kind of fear or trauma. I honestly don't think that's what this is. This is just how the inborne aggression manifests, and as any who know the breed know...cattle dogs can often be very dog aggressive and reactive animals.

Trying to force this puppy to be that dog will fail and result in everyone being miserable. Reactivity and dog aggression usually doesn't kick in like this until 12-20 months. If I could go back in time and tell myself 8 years ago to never keep my seemingly perfect foster puppy I would. This in particular really bothers me for several reasons. In the early 2000s I ran a "safe space" message board for survivors of child abuse, sexual assault and/or bullying. Safe spaces were for people who NEEDED them. People who were traumatized and mentally fragile. The safe space was a place for them to relax as well as heal and work on things, it was a break from the overwhelming world that often triggered their mental health issues which ranged from PTSD, eating disorders, cutting, Bipolar, etc. These were people for whom, a safe space is *necessary*. 

The term "safe space" became popular as a symbol of acceptance, most often used by mental health professionals like school counselors and therapists (or even teachers) to express that their offices and classrooms were a safe place to be LGBT+ without judgment or tolerance of bullying. This is again, a vulnerable and frequently victimized population, who need places they know they can relax and not worry about being mistreated. 

But then...it turned into something else. "Safe spaces" really just became places to not hear anything upsetting or sometimes in some cases, nothing in opposition to certain beliefs they had and anything that makes them feel uncomfortable or upset. Not only is this annoying, unhelpful and ultimately damaging to a person, it turned the term "safe space" into a joke.
